The 201 says CREATING: poll GET /browsers/{id} until it is ACTIVE

get.description:
The session as a listing serves it, and its streams. The automation stream's
status is read from the session itself, and is UNKNOWN when it could not be.
The live view stream endpoint is not opened as is: a viewer opens the url
POST /live-view-stream-sign answers with.
A deleted session is served too: its status says Deleted, and its automation
stream's is UNKNOWN.

delete.description:
Gives the caller's session allowance back. Deleting the browser does the same
for every session that was running on it.

What the session recorded is archived first, and is served afterwards by
GET /browsers/{id}/sessions/{sessionId}/recording. Archiving is best-effort:
the session is deleted even where its recording could not be kept. Sessions
taken down by deleting the browser are not archived.

get.description:
Relays the request to the automation port inside the session, which is where
the browser is driven. The browser must be ACTIVE; one that is still creating
is refused with a 409.

This url is the root of the browser's own devtools api, not a json endpoint of
this service: everything under it is relayed too, on any method, and the reply
is the browser's. A remote devtools client is pointed at this url — it reads
/automation-stream/json/version, and the websocket url it is answered with
points back here rather than into the micro vm.
get.summary: Open the automation stream of a session

parameters.description: Optional. An end user of your own product to scope the call to: sessions created with it are listed and reached only with the same value, and another end user's session is a 404. Without it the call sees every session. 1 to 128 of A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ : @ -
parameters.name: X-End-User-ID

101.description: the connection is relayed to the browser

400.description: the path addressed under the stream leaves the port it is relayed to

409.description: the browser is not active yet

502.description: the session's automation port could not be reached

get.description:
Relays the request to the live view stream port inside the session, where the screen
the browser is drawing on is served over novnc and websockify. The browser must
be ACTIVE; one that is still creating is refused with a 409.

This url is the root of that port rather than a json endpoint of this service:
everything under it is relayed too, on any method. The page is at
/live-view-stream/vnc.html and the connection it opens at /live-view-stream/websockify.

It is not opened directly, and it is not assembled by a caller. A viewer is
authenticated by the url they were given rather than by a header they cannot
send, so the url to open is the one POST /live-view-stream-sign answers with: it
names this page and tells novnc where its websocket connects back, with the
ticket on that address.

What is authenticated is everything that could reach the screen: /websockify,
whose url this service writes, and any other request asking to upgrade, since
the port answers a websocket handshake wherever one arrives. One presenting no
ticket, or none that stands up, is refused with a 403. The page and the novnc
bundle are fetched relatively by the page and can carry no credential, so they
are served to whoever asks for them.
get.summary: Open the live view stream of a session

parameters.description: The ticket, on the /websockify upgrade alone. The signed url puts it there; a caller never does.
parameters.name: t

101.description: the connection is relayed to the browser's screen

200.description: the live view stream port's own reply

400.description: the path addressed under the stream leaves the port it is relayed to

403.description: no ticket on the upgrade, or one that does not stand up

409.description: the browser is not active yet

502.description: the session's live view stream port could not be reached

post.description:
Mints a short-lived url for the live view stream of one session, which is what
a website frames to show a person the screen the browser is drawing on.

The live view is the one url here a person's browser opens rather than an
agent, and a browser can send no portal-user-id header on an iframe load or a
websocket upgrade. So it is authenticated here instead: this call is made for
the caller who owns the browser, and the url it answers with carries a ticket
saying so. The url is used as it is given — as an iframe src — and never
assembled by the caller.

expiresIn bounds opening the url, not watching through it: the iframe spends it
the moment it loads, and the connection it opens runs on past it. What stops
working once it has passed is the reconnect, which is where a page that means to
carry on signs a fresh url and reloads the iframe.
post.summary: Sign a live view stream url

post.description:
name selects the tool and arguments carries that tool's inputs:
executeCode takes language and code, executeCommand and startCommandExecution
take command, listFiles takes directoryPath, writeFiles takes content,
readFiles takes paths, and getTask takes taskId.

The request is held open for as long as the command runs, up to the
configured commandTimeout. startCommandExecution is the exception: it answers
with a task id as soon as the command has started, and getTask is how that
task is followed.

A 400 naming an unsupported tool or language also lists the accepted ones,
beside the message.
post.summary: Invoke a tool inside a session

expiresIn.description:
ExpiresIn is in seconds, and is how long the url may be opened for rather
than how long it may be watched for: the iframe spends it the moment it
loads, and the connection it opens is never re-authenticated.

endUserId.description:
EndUserID is the end user the session was created for, the X-End-User-ID
it was created with. A session created without one is served an empty id,
and is reachable only by a caller that sends none.

name.description:
Name is the caller's own label for the session, stored by the session api
and served back on a listing so that one session can be told from another.
A session created without one is served an empty name.

isError.description:
IsError says whether the content is a failure rather than a result. It is a
pointer because it is stated by the tools whose api states it and left off
entirely by the rest; an absent one reads as false either way.

It is not how a failed invoke is reported: that is answered with a status and
a message by the controller rather than with a 200 carrying a flag. What sets
it is the invoke succeeding and what it answers with not being a result the
caller can act on: the command it ran failed — one stopped at commandTimeout,
or exiting non-zero — or the output came back cut at the buffer's limit. Both
are a 200, and both are the thing a caller cannot tell from the content alone,
since a short answer reads exactly like a whole one.

structuredContent.description:
StructuredContent is the same answer as data, for the part of it a caller acts
on rather than shows a model: the task tools serve the id to poll and the state
it is in there, where the text beside it is what a model reads. It is left off
by the tools that have no such part, since a command's output is text and
nothing else.

BearerAuth.description: VNG Cloud IAM OAuth2 access token, entered as `Bearer <access_token>`. Obtain one by exchanging your service account clientId/clientSecret at the IAM token endpoint (grant_type=client_credentials). The gateway validates it and sets the portal user the request acts for from it.
